title: The Architecture of Attention Why Routines Are Prerequisites for Learning
author: Brendan
summary: Brendan argues that classroom routines—not content—form the invisible instructional infrastructure necessary for student learning. By explicitly teaching procedures through a five-step model (plan, teach, practice, provide feedback, revise), teachers reduce cognitive load and create predictable environments where students focus on learning rather than logistics. The article uses mini-whiteboards as a case study in standardizing even mundane classroom workflows, with practical scripts for teachers.
points: Routines automate behaviors and reduce cognitive load, freeing mental resources for content learning.
Teaching routines requires explicit instruction, modeling, feedback, and revision—not mere verbal directions.
Leaders can codify school-wide routines into an Instructional Playbook to reduce code-switching and create consistency.
Investment in routine-building early in the year yields compound interest in focused attention throughout the year.
quotes: Routines are the building blocks of the classroom culture. They are not merely administrative tasks; they are instructional infrastructure.
Every micro-decision a student has to make—Where do I get a pen? How do I ask for help?—steals precious cognitive bandwidth away from the learning at hand.

By drilling these specific cues like using a '1, 2, 3' finger prompt system, we compress the time spent on logistics. We essentially 'turn back time,' reclaiming minutes every lesson that would otherwise be lost to transition.
Behaviour must be taught, not told. This means applying the same instructional rigour to routines as we do to content.” Archived from Knowledge for Teachers on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
